1	# Global Cost of Living Crisis Index 2026
     2	
     3	## About the Dataset
     4	
     5	This dataset, sourced from Kaggle (alitaqishah/global-cost-of-living-crisis-index-2026), provides a comprehensive snapshot of economic pressure and cost-of-living conditions across **80 major cities** worldwide. Each row represents a single city, with 22 columns capturing cost indices, income levels, rent burdens, inflation rates, and crisis classifications. All index values are benchmarked against New York, USA (index = 100).
     6	
     7	**Key facts:**
     8	- **Rows:** 80 (one per city)
     9	- **Columns:** 22
    10	- **Data year:** 2026
    11	- **Baseline reference:** New York, USA (index = 100)
    12	
    13	## Column Schema
    14	
    15	| Column Name | Type | Description |
    16	|---|---|---|
    17	| rank | Integer | Global rank of the city by cost of living (1 = highest cost) |
    18	| city | String | Name of the city |
    19	| country | String | Country where the city is located |
    20	| region | String | Geographic/economic region (e.g., Western Europe, Asia, Americas) |
    21	| cost_of_living_index | Float | Overall cost of living index relative to New York (100) |
    22	| rent_index | Float | Rent price index relative to New York (100) |
    23	| cost_of_living_plus_rent_index | Float | Combined cost of living and rent index relative to New York (100) |
    24	| groceries_index | Float | Grocery prices index relative to New York (100) |
    25	| restaurant_price_index | Float | Restaurant prices index relative to New York (100) |
    26	| local_purchasing_power_index | Float | Local purchasing power index relative to New York (100); higher values indicate greater purchasing power |
    27	| avg_monthly_net_salary_usd | Integer | Average monthly net salary in USD |
    28	| monthly_rent_1br_city_center_usd | Integer | Monthly rent for a 1-bedroom apartment in the city center, in USD |
    29	| monthly_rent_1br_outside_center_usd | Integer | Monthly rent for a 1-bedroom apartment outside the city center, in USD |
    30	| petrol_price_usd_per_liter | Float | Petrol (gasoline) price in USD per liter |
    31	| annual_inflation_rate_2025_pct | Float | Annual inflation rate as of 2025 (percentage) |
    32	| population_city_millions | Float | City population in millions |
    33	| cost_crisis_tier | Integer | Numeric tier classifying the severity of the cost-of-living crisis (lower values may indicate affluent/high-cost cities; higher values indicate more severe crisis conditions) |
    34	| crisis_label | String | Descriptive label for the crisis tier (e.g., "Affluent – High Cost", and other categories indicating varying levels of economic stress) |
    35	| oil_shock_exposure | String | Categorical assessment of the city's vulnerability to oil price shocks (e.g., "Low", "Medium", "High") |
    36	| rent_to_salary_ratio_pct | Float | Percentage of average monthly salary consumed by city-center 1BR rent; higher values indicate greater rent burden |
    37	| data_year | Integer | Year the data represents (all values are 2026) |
    38	| baseline_city | String | Reference city for all index calculations ("New York, USA (index=100)") |
    39	
    40	## Key Analytical Notes
    41	
    42	- **Index interpretation:** All index columns (cost_of_living_index, rent_index, groceries_index, restaurant_price_index, local_purchasing_power_index, and the combined index) are relative to New York City = 100. Values above 100 indicate higher costs (or greater purchasing power) than New York; values below 100 indicate lower.
    43	- **Crisis classification:** The `cost_crisis_tier` (integer) and `crisis_label` (string) columns together classify each city's economic stress level. Analysts should examine the distribution of these tiers to understand how many cities fall into each category.
    44	- **Rent burden:** The `rent_to_salary_ratio_pct` is a pre-calculated metric that directly measures housing affordability. Values above 50% are generally considered severe.
    45	- **Oil shock exposure:** This categorical variable (Low/Medium/High) can be cross-referenced with inflation and cost indices to assess vulnerability.
    46	- **Data quality:** The dataset is compiled for analytical and educational purposes and may include estimated or aggregated values. The `data_year` and `baseline_city` columns are constant across all rows (2026 and New York respectively). No missing values are indicated in the schema, but analysts should verify completeness during processing.
    47	- **Scope:** With 80 cities across multiple regions, the dataset enables both city-level deep dives and region-level aggregations.

Executive Overview

The global cost-of-living landscape in 2026 reveals a stark divergence between affluent, high-wage cities and those gripped by acute affordability crises. Among the 80 major cities analyzed, 19 cities (24%) fall into the most severe crisis tier (Tier 5), where residents face extreme rent burdens, collapsing purchasing power, or hyperinflationary conditions. At the opposite end, Swiss cities dominate the top ranks by absolute cost, yet their elevated salaries keep rent burdens manageable.

Headline: The crisis is not uniformly about high prices. It is about the disconnect between prices and incomes. Zurich is the most expensive city but maintains a lower rent-to-salary ratio (70.8%) than Manila (55.1%) because salaries scale with costs. Cairo, by contrast, has the lowest cost-of-living index (26.0) yet still extracts 53.1% of a meager income for rent.

Key extremes:

  • Most expensive: Zurich (118.5), Geneva (116.5), Basel (112.4)
  • Least expensive: Kathmandu (24.0), Cairo (26.0), Lahore (26.0)
  • Highest rent burden: Zurich (70.8%), Geneva (70.2%), Seattle (71.2%)
  • Lowest rent burden: Lahore (51.0%), Casablanca (51.9%), Dhaka (51.4%)
  • Highest inflation: Buenos Aires (150.0%), Beirut (50.0%), Istanbul (47.0%)
  • Lowest inflation: Shanghai (0.9%), Beijing (0.9%), Bangkok (1.5%)

Regional Cost-of-Living Comparison

Regional averages mask significant internal variation. Western Europe and North America cluster at the high-cost end, while South Asia and Africa sit at the bottom. However, outliers within each region are often more policy-relevant than the averages themselves.

Regional Outliers

East Asia — Shanghai vs. Seoul: Both have similar cost-of-living indices (~60 and 59), but Shanghai's inflation is 0.9% versus Seoul's 2.1%. Shanghai's rent-to-salary ratio (61.8%) is also lower than Seoul's (63.9%), driven by lower salaries in Shanghai offset by even lower rent.
Middle East — Beirut: At 42.0, Beirut's cost index is below the regional average, yet its 50.0% inflation and 35.0 PPP index make it the most stressed city in the region by far.
Western Europe — Milan: Milan's PPP index (83.5) is a dramatic outlier in a region where most cities exceed 110. Combined with a 62.1% rent burden, it is the most stressed city in Western Europe.
North America — New York vs. Houston: New York is the benchmark (100), while Houston sits at 70.5 with a 140.0 PPP index and a lower rent burden (63.1%), making it one of the most affordable major US cities on an income-adjusted basis.

Regional Distribution of Crisis Tiers

Affordability and Rent Burden Analysis

Housing cost as a share of income is the single most actionable metric for policymakers. Across all 80 cities, the average rent-to-salary ratio is 60.4%, meaning the typical city-center 1-bedroom apartment consumes more than half of the average net salary. In 23 cities, this ratio exceeds 65%, and in 7 cities it exceeds 70%.

Critical Threshold: A rent-to-salary ratio above 50% is widely considered severe. In this dataset, 69 of 80 cities (86%) exceed this threshold, indicating a global affordability emergency.

Pattern: The scatter plot reveals two distinct clusters. High-salary cities (USD 4,000+) cluster in the upper-right with rent burdens of 62–72%. Low-salary cities (USD <1,500) cluster in the lower-left, where even modest rents (USD 300–700) consume 50–58% of income. The policy implication is clear: in high-salary cities, the problem is absolute rent levels; in low-salary cities, it is income inadequacy.

Crisis Tier Profiling

Each city is classified into one of five crisis tiers based on a composite of cost indices, rent burden, purchasing power, and inflation. The tiers range from Tier 1 (affluent, high-cost but manageable) to Tier 5 (severe crisis conditions).

Average Indicators by Crisis Tier

What Separates High-Crisis from Affluent Cities?

Affluent Cities (Tier 1):

  • Cost-of-living index averages 104.5 (above New York)
  • Purchasing power index averages 162.0 — the highest of any tier
  • Inflation is low (1.5% average)
  • Rent burden is high in absolute terms (68.8%) but offset by very high salaries
  • Examples: Zurich, Geneva, Basel, Doha, Riyadh

Severe Crisis Cities (Tier 5):

  • Cost-of-living index averages only 33.3 (well below New York)
  • Purchasing power index collapses to 50.2
  • Inflation averages 29.5% — nearly 20× the affluent tier
  • Rent burden is lower in percentage terms (54.2%) but catastrophic in real terms given near-subsistence incomes
  • Examples: Beirut, Manila, Kyiv, Accra, Lagos, Colombo, Buenos Aires, Mumbai, Delhi, Dhaka, Karachi, Cairo, Lahore, Kathmandu
Key Insight: The defining feature of Tier 5 is not high prices — it is eroded purchasing power combined with high or hyperinflation. A policy focused only on rent controls in these cities would miss the larger macroeconomic instability driving the crisis.

Inflation and Oil Shock Exposure

External economic shocks — particularly oil price volatility — compound cost-of-living stress. Cities classified as having High oil shock exposure tend to cluster in the Middle East, Southeast Asia, and Africa, where fuel subsidies are limited and transport costs weigh heavily on household budgets.

Most Vulnerable Cities

High Oil + High Inflation: Istanbul (47.0% inflation, High oil exposure), Accra (18.0%, High), Kyiv (14.5%, High), and Karachi (28.5%, High) face a double shock where both fuel and general prices are spiraling.
High Oil + Low Inflation (resilient): Singapore (2.3% inflation, High oil exposure) and Riyadh (2.2%, High) demonstrate that high oil exposure does not automatically translate to crisis when fiscal buffers and subsidy regimes are strong.
Low Oil + High Inflation (idiosyncratic): Buenos Aires (150.0% inflation, Low oil exposure) and Moscow (9.5%, Low) show that inflation can be domestically driven by monetary or sanctions-related factors independent of oil markets.

Purchasing Power vs. Inflation

Key Findings and Policy Implications

Critical Findings

  1. The crisis is income-driven, not price-driven, in the Global South. Cities like Cairo, Lagos, and Dhaka have cost-of-living indices below 30, yet residents spend 50–55% of tiny incomes on rent. Interventions must prioritize income support and macroeconomic stabilization over price controls.
  2. Western Europe and North America face an absolute housing shortage. Rent burdens above 65% in Swiss and US cities signal insufficient supply relative to demand. Zoning reform, social housing investment, and tenancy protections are the most levers.
  3. Hyperinflation is concentrated but catastrophic. Only 5 cities have inflation above 25%, but they house over 80 million people. Currency stabilization and central bank independence are prerequisites for any sustainable affordability policy.
  4. Oil exposure amplifies risk where fiscal capacity is weak. High oil exposure combined with high inflation defines the most vulnerable cities. Targeted fuel subsidies or public transport investment can buffer the poorest households.
  5. Purchasing power is the best predictor of lived experience. The 141.7-point gap between Basel (183.7) and Cairo (42.0) in purchasing power index explains more about quality of life than the 86.4-point gap in cost-of-living index.

Areas for Further Research

  • Intra-city inequality: City-level averages mask neighborhood-level extremes. Sub-city data on rent burdens by income decile would sharpen targeting.
  • Policy intervention tracking: A longitudinal panel measuring which policies (rent control, housing vouchers, zoning reform) most effectively reduce rent-to-salary ratios.
  • Remittance dependence: Several Tier 5 cities (e.g., Manila, Dhaka, Karachi) are heavily remittance-dependent. The impact of exchange-rate shifts on real household income deserves deeper analysis.
  • Climate vulnerability intersection: Cities with high oil exposure and low fiscal capacity are often also climate-vulnerable. Integrated stress-testing of combined shocks would inform adaptive social protection.
